abstract-title: "Abstract"
abstract: |
  The gradient projection algorithm (GPA) is the most used tool to rotate factor models. However, GPA is currently limited to fully orthogonal or fully oblique solutions. Keeping structural zeros in selected positions of the factor correlation matrix after rotation is currently unavailable. This limitation is relevant to analyses where theoretical considerations or study design require certain factor correlations to be zero. We therefore introduce the orthoblique rotation, which allows orthogonal and oblique relations between factors to coexist. Building on Jennrich's algorithms, we describe the geometric foundations of GPA and extend them to the orthoblique rotation. We illustrate its usefulness for exploratory bifactor models with multiple correlated general factors that remain orthogonal to group factors, and for multitrait–multimethod models in which trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets while remaining orthogonal between sets. Finally, we make available the new orthoblique rotation in the R package \texttt{latent} through the \texttt{lrotate()} function, which extends the capabilities of the popular \texttt{GPArotation} package of Bernaards and Jennrich (2005). Taken together, this work helps bridge the gap between exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and continues Jennrich's efforts to expand the flexibility and scope of factor rotation.
  
  Keywords: bifactor, exploratory factor analysis, factor rotation, gradient projection algorithm, orthoblique rotation
---

# Introduction

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is a popular framework for estimating large and complex factor structures. It surpasses the overly restrictive measurement models and the unacceptable model fit indices often encountered in applications of confirmatory factor analysis [CFA; @marsh_2020]. In CFA, incorrectly fixing cross-loadings to zero is an important caveat whereas EFA permits the estimation of all the loading parameters of the measurement model by means of a rotation step, reducing the risk of model misspecification.

However, the flexibility of EFA comes at the expense of specifying a suitable simplicity criterion to be optimized, so that a factor solution is rotated to a loading matrix that best approximates the desired simple structure. In this regard, the gradient projection algorithm [GPA; @jennrich_2001; @jennrich_2002] has been the predominant computational tool for rotating loading patterns during the last twenty years. The success of GPA is instantiated by its availability in widely used and reputed statistical programs such as Mplus [@mplus], \texttt{lavaan} [@lavaan], and \texttt{psych} [@psych]. In contrast with previously used rotation procedures like the criterion-specific pairwise algorithms discussed by @jennrich_2001, GPA is simple and elegant. In fact, a general-purpose optimization routine based on GPA can be written in about 50 lines of code in the R language ^[See the \texttt{GPForth} and \texttt{GPFoblq} functions from the \texttt{GPArotation} R package [@bernaards_2005] for orthogonal and oblique rotation, respectively.]. Moreover, GPA is based on an optimization framework where traditional search directions based on first- and second-order derivatives and step-size selection techniques like backtracking line-search can be used [@liu_2021].

The generality of GPA for factor rotation was the main contribution of @jennrich_2001 and @jennrich_2002. Rather than developing a different algorithm for every simplicity criterion, Jennrich showed that a common computational procedure could optimize many criteria under the same rotation constraints. Bernaards and Jennrich (2005) developed this idea into general-purpose software and separated the evaluation of the criterion and the gradient of the parameters from the operations that enforce the rotation constraints. They also provided derivations, proofs, and software implementation details. Thus, their work provided both the motivation and the computational starting point for the present generalization to a new rotation method. Our purpose is to give a deeper and more explicit geometric account of all the mathematical objects involving factor rotation and the connections between them. Explaining why they are needed, how they are derived from the constraints of the rotation matrix, and how they work together provides a constructive route from the orthogonal and oblique cases to other rotation geometries.

This generalization is very important in EFA because the applications of GPA are currently limited to either orthogonal or oblique rotation. In other words, all the factors in an EFA model are currently constrained to be either orthogonal or allowed to correlate. This circumstance is problematic in cases where the researchers know in advance that two sets of factors may be correlated within each set but orthogonal between sets. For example, consider multitrait-multimethod models, in which trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets but trait–method correlations must be constrained to zero by design. In this scenario, there should be structural zeros in the factor correlation matrix to effectively separate the variance explained by traits and methods. In other cases, it may be desirable to constrain one factor, or a group of factors, to be orthogonal to the remaining factors in order to obtain a more parsimonious pattern structure. For this scenario, consider applications of exploratory bifactor modeling with one or multiple general factors in which all the general factors must be orthogonal to the group factors, but may be correlated among themselves [@jimenez_2023a; @jimenez_2023b]. If the general factors were allowed to correlate with the group factors in an oblique rotation analysis, then the variance explained by each kind of factor could not be correctly disentangled and would complicate the interpretation of the general-factor loadings.

Thereby, a generalization of the oblique and orthogonal rotations that allows for a mix of oblique and orthogonal factors could aid the correct estimation and interpretation of such factor structures. An illustrative example of this generalization is presented in Figure \ref{fig:rotations} along with the standard orthogonal and oblique cases.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=1\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{"figures/manifolds.pdf"}
\caption{\fontsize{12}{12}\selectfont Factor correlation matrices expected for six factors after orthogonal, oblique, and orthoblique rotations. Asterisks indicate freely estimated correlations.}
\label{fig:rotations}
\end{figure}

In the orthoblique example presented in the figure, factors are organized into two oblique blocks of two factors each, with the remaining two factors being completely orthogonal. However, other correlation patterns are possible by modifying the size of the oblique and orthogonal blocks of factors. As such, the distinctive feature of the orthoblique rotation is that some blocks of factors may be allowed to correlate within but not between. 

The objectives of this work are fourfold. First, we give a coherent and self-contained explanation of EFA and GPA for orthogonal and oblique rotation, connecting the matrix formulas of @jennrich_2001 and @jennrich_2002 with their underlying geometry. Second, using these explanations, we derive the orthoblique rotation, a generalization in which both oblique and orthogonal relations between factors coexist, and show how the conventional oblique and orthogonal rotations are obtained as special cases. We also discuss how to obtain standard errors for the rotated parameters. Third, we make this new rotation available in the \texttt{latent} R package and explain how the function \texttt{lrotate()} extends the rotation framework used in \texttt{GPArotation}. In addition, we provide the more general \texttt{lefa()} function to conduct EFA. Lastly, we illustrate the usefulness of this generalization in two empirical examples concerning exploratory multitrait-multimethod and bifactor models with multiple general factors. In the end, we discuss the benefits of the orthoblique rotation for preserving the flexibility of EFA to uncover cross-loadings and departures from theoretical expectations while retaining a desired factor-correlation pattern with structural zeros.

# Factor rotation

In EFA, the covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ among the observed items is modeled as a function of the factor loading matrix $\mathbf{\Lambda}$, the factor correlation matrix $\mathbf{\Psi}$, and the error covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}$. The loading matrix contains the relationships between the observed items and the common factors, the factor correlation matrix describes the associations among these factors, and the error covariance matrix is assumed to be diagonal, containing the error variances or uniquenesses.

EFA is usually performed in two steps. First, an identified model $\mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{\Lambda}_0^\top + \mathbf{\Theta}$ is estimated by maximum likelihood or least squares, where $\mathbf{\Lambda}_0$ is a loading matrix constrained to have either orthogonal columns or a lower-triangular structure. Second, $\mathbf{\Lambda}_0$ is rotated to find an alternative but equally fitting model $\mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Psi}\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top + \mathbf{\Theta}$, where $\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}^{-\top}$ and $\mathbf{\Psi} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$. This last step involves finding the optimal rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$ that minimizes a complexity criterion seeking to obtain a sparse and interpretable $\mathbf{\Lambda}$. However, $\mathbf{X}$ must be subject to certain constraints that distinguish orthogonal from oblique rotations. In orthogonal rotation, the constraint is $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}$, whereas in oblique rotation it is $\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{1}$. Therefore, both orthogonal and oblique rotation matrices belong to smooth nonlinear sets of $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ matrices characterized by these specific constraints. Informally, these specific sets are termed manifolds and denoted by $\mathcal{M}$.

The problem of factor rotation is that the optimal orthogonal or oblique rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$ cannot generally be found by using ordinary optimization algorithms that do not enforce these constraints. For this purpose, the Gradient Projection Algorithm (GPA) has proved to be an elegant and robust solution. GPA builds on differential geometry to perform optimization on nonlinear manifolds. Let $\tilde{f}$ be a complexity function with domain in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ that we aim to minimize with respect to a rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$. This function can be any complexity criterion, such as varimax, oblimin, or geomin. Suppose that we want to constrain the solution to lie on a nonlinear manifold $\mathcal{M}$ characterized by a defining smooth function $h:\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ that satisfies

$$
\mathcal{M} = h^{-1}(\mathbf{0}) = \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{0} \right\},
$$

so that any matrix $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$ implies $h(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{0}$. Here, $d$ is the number of independent constraints defining the manifold. This means that, in the orthogonal case, $h$ collects the $n(n+1)/2$ distinct constraints of the symmetric matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{I}$, whereas in the oblique case it collects the $n$ diagonal constraints. In this manner, the orthogonal and oblique manifolds can be stated as the sets of full-rank $\mathbf{X}$ matrices satisfying the following conditions, respectively:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{O}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{0} \right\}, \\
\mathcal{OB}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X}) = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})-\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0} \right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

<!-- Because these constraints are smooth and their differentials have full rank at every point of the manifolds, the regular level-set theorem guarantees that these sets are smooth embedded manifolds.^[That is, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}))=d$ for all $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$ [@boumal_2023, Sections 3.2 and 7.7].] -->

To better understand these manifold definitions, an illustration of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds for $n=3$ is presented in Figure \ref{fig:orthogonal-oblique-manifolds}. In both manifolds, each column $\mathbf{x}_j$ of the rotation matrix is a unit vector and can therefore be represented on the unit sphere. The oblique manifold is the product of $n$ unit spheres, whereas the orthogonal manifold is the subset of this product in which the vectors are also constrained to point in mutually perpendicular directions.

Visually, the GPA consists of moving these vectors across the surface of the unit sphere until the complexity criterion $\tilde{f}$ is minimized, subject to the additional perpendicularity constraints in orthogonal rotation. To move the vectors in this way while minimizing $\tilde{f}$, small steps must be taken through an iterative algorithm. However, this is not trivial. At iteration $k$, traditional unconstrained optimization algorithms usually compute a new candidate as
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = \mathbf{X}_k + t_k\mathbf{V}_k,
$$ {#eq-updating}

where $\mathbf{V}_k$ is a direction along which the complexity function decreases and $t_k$ is a step size. In gradient descent, for example, $\mathbf{V}_k = -\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)$, where $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)$ is the Euclidean gradient in the unrestricted space $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$.^[The Euclidean gradient is characterized by $\mathrm{D}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}] = \langle \mathbf{V},\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)\rangle$ for any $\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, with $\langle ., . \rangle$ denoting the Frobenius inner product.] The problem is that this updating scheme does not guarantee that the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ remains on the manifold, not even when $\mathbf{X}_k$ already belongs to it. Furthermore, the descent direction $\mathbf{V}_k$ is also unrestricted in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and is not necessarily a valid descent direction on a nonlinear manifold. In other words, a straight-line displacement in the Euclidean space, as shown in the updating @eq-updating, is not generally a feasible displacement on a nonlinear manifold.

Hence, the GPA solves two problems: (1) proposing an appropriate descent direction $\mathbf{V}_k$ on $\mathcal{M}$ and (2) securing that, after moving along this direction, the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ remains on $\mathcal{M}$.

# Solution to problem 1: the Riemannian gradient

The Riemannian gradient is a generalization of the Euclidean gradient that represents first-order directions on a manifold. As such, its negative provides valid descent direction along manifolds like the spheres depicted in Figure \ref{fig:orthogonal-oblique-manifolds}. More precisely, the Riemannian gradient is characterized as follows [@boumal_2023, Definition 3.58]:

\begin{definition}
The Riemannian gradient of $f$ at $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$, denoted by $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$, is the unique element of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ that satisfies $\mathrm{D}f(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \left\langle \mathbf{V}, \text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) \right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}$ for every $\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$.
\label{def:riemannian-gradient}
\end{definition}

<!-- @absil_2009, Definition 3.31;  -->
<!-- [@absil_2009, Equation 3.37; @boumal_2023, Proposition 3.61]. -->

<!-- The negative Riemannian gradient is a descent direction because -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \begin{aligned} -->
<!-- \mathrm{D}f(\mathbf{X}) -->
<!-- \left[ -->
<!-- -\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) -->
<!-- \right] -->
<!-- &= -->
<!-- \left\langle -->
<!-- -\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}), -->
<!-- \text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) -->
<!-- \right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}} -->
<!-- \\ -->
<!-- &= -->
<!-- - -->
<!-- \left\| -->
<!-- \text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) -->
<!-- \right\|_{\mathbf{X}}^2 -->
<!-- \leq -->
<!-- 0. -->
<!-- \end{aligned} -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- The inequality is strict whenever $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})\neq\mathbf{0}$. Therefore, the first task of the GPA is to replace the negative Euclidean gradient with the negative Riemannian gradient, which is a valid tangent descent direction. -->

Informally, if we zoom in enough around a point $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$, eventually everything looks linear.^[As an analogy, the Earth is round but locally everything looks flat.] Thus, an idea to move over $\mathcal{M}$ consists of finding tangent directions to $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$ that look linear from an infinitesimal point of view. 

Consider doing a first-order Taylor expansion of $h$ around the current candidate $\mathbf{X}_k$,
$$
h(\mathbf{X}_k+t\mathbf{V}_k) \approx h(\mathbf{X}_k) + t\,\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}_k].
$$ {#eq-taylor}
Because we can always propose a candidate $\mathbf{X}_k$ that already belongs to $\mathcal{M}$ ^[We can always propose an initial starting point $\mathbf{X}_1 \in \mathcal{M}$.], it follows that $h(\mathbf{X}_k) = \mathbf{0}$. Then, we may choose a $\mathbf{V}_k$ such that $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}_k] = \mathbf{0}$, so that @eq-taylor becomes $\mathbf{0}$ and we preserve the manifold constraints to first order. Therefore, appropriate directions to move along the manifolds constitute the kernel of $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)$:
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M} \equiv \ker\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}) = \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \mathbf{0} \right\},
$$
where the subscript $k$ is dropped hereafter for clarity and generality. The set $\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$ is known as the tangent space of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathcal{M}$. In other words, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ is the set of all infinitesimally feasible directions at $\mathbf{X}$ that are linear. This linearity property is important because it allows traditional optimization algorithms that work in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ to be used in the GPA framework.

Connecting this notion of linear space to our previous examples, the tangent spaces of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds at any $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$ can be stated as the collection of directions for which the differentials of their respective defining functions are $\mathbf{0}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0} \right\}, \\
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{0} \right\},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-tangent_space}
where $\mathrm{ddiag}$ is an operator that sets the off-diagonal entries of a matrix to zero.

Notice that tangent spaces can be viewed as a collection of the $n^2-d$ free components in the manifolds, so that $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n)) = n(n-1)/2$ is the number of free elements in an orthogonal matrix and $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)) = n(n-1)$ is the number of free elements in an oblique matrix. Thereby, we can exploit the above differentials to parameterize the tangent spaces in such a way that the parameterizations preserve the tangent space dimension.

In the orthogonal case, for instance, if we set $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X\Omega}$, then by substitution in @eq-tangent_space, we have
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n) = \left\{ \mathbf{X\Omega}: \mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top = \mathbf{0} \right\}.
$$
This is a valid full-rank parameterization of the tangent space of the orthogonal manifold because $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is a skew-symmetric matrix and hence it has $n(n-1)/2$ free elements.

In the oblique case, for a nonsingular rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$, a useful full-rank parameterization of the tangent space is $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}^{-\top} \mathbf{\Omega}$, which by substitution in @eq-tangent_space yields
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)
=
\left\{
\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}:
\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Omega})
=
\mathbf{0}
\right\}.
$$
Indeed, $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is an arbitrary off-diagonal matrix with $n(n-1)$ free elements and thus it is a valid full-rank parameterization of the tangent space of the oblique manifold.

Now, notice that any member of $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ can be decomposed in orthogonal complements. At any point $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$, the Euclidean space can be decomposed into the orthogonal direct sum of the tangent and normal spaces,
$$
\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
=
\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}
\oplus
\mathcal{N}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}.
$$

If this $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ element is the Euclidean gradient of $\tilde{f}$ at $\mathbf{X}$, this means that it can be decomposed into an element belonging to the tangent space, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$, and another belonging to the normal space, $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$. Therefore, there must exist orthogonal complements satisfying

$$
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel + \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp,
$$ {#eq-orth_compl_grad}

where $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel$ and $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp$ are the projections of $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})$ onto the tangent and normal spaces of the manifold $\mathcal{M}$, respectively [@absil_2009, p. 47]. Figure \ref{fig:tangent-gradient} depicts the relationship between these quantities.

As shown in Figure \ref{fig:tangent-gradient}, a tangent space is indeed a linearization of the manifold at a given $\mathbf{X}$. At this point, the Euclidean gradient can be decomposed into orthogonal components as expressed in @eq-orth_compl_grad: one belonging to the tangent space and another belonging to the normal space. However, to make sense of this notion of orthogonality at any $\mathbf{V} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$, we must endow the tangent space with a metric, like the Frobenius inner product (i.e., $\langle \mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{V})$). Under this metric, we can formalize the orthogonality of every vector in the tangent space with a vector in the normal space, so the collection of these inner products over all tangent spaces defines a Riemannian metric on $\mathcal{M}$, turning it into a Riemannian manifold. This structure provides the geometric foundation for defining the Riemannian gradient.

Let $f=\tilde{f}|_{\mathcal{M}}$ be the restriction of the complexity criterion $\tilde{f}$ to a manifold. Using @eq-orth_compl_grad and the Frobenius inner product as Riemannian metric, we arrive at the following identities for any $\mathbf{V} \in \mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle
\mathbf{V},
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel
\right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left[
\mathbf{V}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp
\right)
\right]
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right)
-
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp
\right)
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right),
\quad
\text{because }
\mathbf{V}
\text{ is orthogonal to }
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp,
\\
&=
\mathrm{D}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}],
\quad
\text{by the definition of the Euclidean gradient},
\\
&=
\mathrm{D}f(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}],
\quad
\text{because }
f=\tilde{f}|_{\mathcal{M}}
\text{ and }
\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M} \\
&= \left\langle
\mathbf{V},
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
\right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality follows directly from the definition of the Riemannian gradient (\ref{def:riemannian-gradient}). And from the preceding identities, this element turns out to be $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel$, the projection of the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space of $\mathcal{M}$.

There can be many ways to find a formula for the Riemannian gradient, but a good strategy consists of obtaining an expression for $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp \in \mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ and substituting this into @eq-orth_compl_grad.

In the cases of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds, recall that the parameterizations of the tangent spaces were $\mathbf{X\Omega}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$, respectively, so their corresponding normal spaces must be
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n)
&=
\left\{
\mathbf{N}:
\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
\quad
\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}^\top
\right\},
\\
\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)
&=
\left\{
\mathbf{N}:
\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
\quad
\mathbf{A}
\text{ is diagonal}
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ 
Clearly, the tangent and normal parameterizations are orthogonal in each scenario. In the orthogonal manifold, for any skew-symmetric $\mathbf{\Omega}$ and symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ we have $\langle \mathbf{X\Omega}, \mathbf{XA} \rangle = 0$. In the oblique manifold, for an off-diagonal $\mathbf{\Omega}$ and diagonal $\mathbf{A}$ we have $\langle \mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}, \mathbf{XA} \rangle = 0$. Therefore, in both cases the tangent and normal parameterizations are orthogonal complements and, using @eq-orth_compl_grad, the Riemannian gradient can be written as
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
=
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
$$ {#eq-riemannian_param}
where $\mathbf{A}$ must be chosen so that $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ belongs to the corresponding tangent space.

For orthogonal rotation, the Riemannian gradient must satisfy the tangent space equation
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})^\top\mathbf{X}
=
\mathbf{0}.
$$

Substituting $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ by the orthogonal complements parameterization in @eq-riemannian_param gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
+
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)^\top
\mathbf{X}
&= \mathbf{0}
\\
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
-
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
-
\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}
&= \mathbf{0}, \quad \text{and}
\\
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
-
2\mathbf{A}
&= \mathbf{0}, \quad \text{because } \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I} \text{ and } \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}^\top.
\end{aligned}
$$
It then follows that
$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
\right].
$$

Finally, defining $\mathrm{sym}(\mathbf{B})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B}^\top\right)$, we have $\mathbf{A}=\mathrm{sym}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})\right)$ and the Riemannian gradient for orthogonal rotation becomes
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) = \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) -
\mathbf{X}\, \mathrm{sym}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) \right).
$$

On the other hand, for oblique rotation, the Riemannian gradient must satisfy the tangent space equation
$$
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
\right]
=
\mathbf{0}.
$$

Substituting again $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ for the orthogonal complements parameterization in @eq-riemannian_param gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
\right]
&= \mathbf{0}
\\
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right]
-
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left(
\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
&= \mathbf{0}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $\mathbf{A}$ is diagonal and $\mathrm{ddiag}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)=\mathbf{I}$, we get $\mathbf{A} = \mathrm{ddiag}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}\right)$.

Therefore,
$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right],
$$

and the Riemannian gradient for oblique rotation becomes
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
=
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right].
$$

These are indeed the same projected-gradient formulas denoted by \texttt{Gp} in the orthogonal and oblique implementations of Bernaards and Jennrich (pp. 692--695; 2005) and in the \texttt{GPArotation} package.

# Solution to problem 2: the retraction

With this generalization of gradients to nonlinear manifolds, we are prepared to compute valid descent directions along the tangent space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$. However, we are not ready to compute valid candidates because the update
$$
\mathbf{Z}_{k+1} = \mathbf{X}_k-t_k\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k)
$$ {#eq-tangent_step}

does not generally belong to $\mathcal{M}$, however small $t_k$ is. The tangent direction only provides a first-order linear approximation to the manifold at $\mathbf{X}_k$, as we showed before in @eq-taylor. This means that the condition $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}]=\mathbf{0}$ does not generally imply that the tangent step $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V}$ lies exactly on $\mathcal{M}$ for a nonzero $t$. It only ensures that the constraints are preserved to first order. To see this, let's take the crossproduct of the tangent step $\mathbf{Z}$ to check how it departs from the manifold constraints:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z} &=
(\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})^\top (\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V}) \\
&= \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + t(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X}) + t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$
In orthogonal rotation, the term $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X}$ vanishes because $\mathbf{V}$ was chosen precisely to satisfy the tangent equation for the orthogonal manifold (@eq-tangent_space) and we are left with
$$
\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{I} + t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}.
$$ {#eq-cross_step_orth}

This means that with the updating scheme in @eq-tangent_step, the orthogonality constraint is violated by the residual $t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}$. Following the same argument in the case of the oblique manifold, we have
$$
\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{I} + t^2\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}),
$$ {#eq-cross_step_oblq}
and the unit norm constraint would be off by a factor of $t^2\text{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})$. 

Mapping the tangent step back to the manifold is the second problem addressed by the GPA. After taking a step $t$ along the negative Riemannian gradient, the resulting point must be projected back onto the manifold while preserving the direction of the tangent step. For this purpose, suppose that we apply some projection $R_\mathbf{X}:\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}$ that restores the constraints exactly while preserving this direction. Because the tangent step is already correct to first order, $R_\mathbf{X}$ only needs to act on the higher-order residuals of @eq-cross_step_orth and @eq-cross_step_oblq. This is exactly what a retraction does: it fixes the constraints of the tangent step $\mathbf{Z}$ without modifying the descent direction (i.e., the negative of the Riemannian gradient).

A retraction only needs to satisfy two conditions. The first condition ensures that taking a zero step leaves the current point unchanged. In other words, if we do not move $\mathbf{X}$ along any direction, then the projection must return the same $\mathbf{X}$. The second condition recognizes that the tangent step $\mathbf{X} + t\mathbf{V}$ already satisfies the manifold constraints to first order because $\mathbf{V}$ was picked to satisfy the tangent space equations. Therefore it requires that $R_{\mathbf{X}}(t\mathbf{V})$ has the same initial direction $\mathbf{V}$ as the tangent step. In other words, a retraction restores the manifold constraints exactly without changing the first-order direction on the manifold so that the Riemannian gradient is still the descent direction. 

Using these conditions, we can define a retraction in the following manner [@boumal_2023, Definition 3.47]:

\begin{definition}
\label{retraction_definition}
A retraction is a smooth map
$R_\mathbf{X}:\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}$ that satisfies the following conditions: \\
(1) $R_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{X}$, and \\
(2) $DR_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{0})[\mathbf{V}]=\mathbf{V}$ for every
$\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$.
\end{definition}

<!-- Both requirements can equivalently be stated by considering the curve -->
<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \gamma(t)=R_\mathbf{X}(t\mathbf{V}), -->
<!-- $$ -->
<!-- which satisfies $\gamma(0)=\mathbf{X}$ and $\gamma^\prime(0)=\mathbf{V}$. -->

<!-- Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a smooth map from an ambient neighborhood of $\mathbf{X}$ into the manifold. Suppose that $\mathcal P(\mathbf{Y})=\mathbf{Y}$ for every nearby $\mathbf{Y} \in\mathcal M$. Then $R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf V)=\mathcal P(\mathbf X+\mathbf V)$ defines a local retraction. Since $\mathcal P$ leaves manifold points unchanged, $\mathcal P(\gamma(t))=\gamma(t)$. Differentiating this identity at zero yields $\mathrm D\mathcal P(\mathbf X)[\mathbf V] = \mathbf V$. The chain rule then gives $\mathrm D R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf0)[\mathbf V] = \mathrm D\mathcal P(\mathbf X)[\mathbf V] = \mathbf V$. Also, $R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf0)=\mathcal P(\mathbf X)=\mathbf X$. That proves both conditions. -->

Combining the Riemannian gradient with a retraction, the valid updating equation that GPA uses becomes
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = R_{\mathbf{X}_k} \left(-t_k\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k) \right).
$$ {#eq-gpa_update}

Hence, the Riemannian gradient determines a valid descent direction in the tangent space, whereas the retraction guarantees that the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ belongs to $\mathcal{M}$ after correcting the higher-order imprecisions of the tangent step. Figure \ref{fig:retraction} gives a notion of how a tangent step is retracted onto the manifold.

                  .. controls (1.65,-1.25) and (-1.75,-1.35) .. cycle;
  \draw[thick] (-3.0,-0.65) .. controls (-1.8,1.20) and (1.4,1.10) .. (3.0,-0.25);
  \draw[thick] (-3.0,-0.65) .. controls (-1.60,-1.45) and (1.60,-1.20) .. (3.0,-0.25);

  \node at (-2.30,-0.48) {$\mathcal{M}$};

Starting from $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$, a tangent step is taken along the negative Riemannian gradient in the tangent space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$. Since the point $\mathbf{X}-t\,\operatorname{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ does not generally belong to the manifold, the retraction maps it back onto $\mathcal{M}$.}

For orthogonal rotation, a suitable retraction is obtained by applying the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to the columns of $\mathbf{Z}$ such that $R_\mathbf{X}^{\text{orth}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{Q}$, where $\mathbf{Q}$ is the orthonormal matrix of the QR decomposition of the tangent step $\mathbf{Z}$, with the triangular factor chosen to have positive diagonal entries. Alternatively, if $\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}^\top$ is a singular value decomposition, another valid retraction is $R_\mathbf{X}^{\text{orth}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{W}^\top$. This is actually the orthogonal projection used in the algorithms of @jennrich_2001 and Bernaards and Jennrich (2005). The QR and singular value decomposition retractions need not produce the same finite update, but both are smooth operations that satisfy the conditions in Definition \ref{retraction_definition}, leaving the point $\mathbf{X}$ unchanged when no direction is applied and preserving the tangent direction to first order.

Let's define the retraction for orthogonal rotation as
$$
R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{orth}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{Z} \left(\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z}\right)^{-1/2},
$$ {#eq-orth_retraction}
which is equivalent to the singular value decomposition method.

The first condition of Definition \ref{retraction_definition} is met because at $t=0$, we have $R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{X}$ as $\mathbf{X}$ is already orthonormal. To check the second condition, we can rewrite the retraction in terms of @eq-cross_step_orth as follows:
$$
R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{orth}}(t\mathbf{V}) = (\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}\right)^{-1/2}.
$$
Then the derivative of this expression with respect to $t$ becomes
$$
\frac{d}{dt}R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{orth}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{V}\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}\right)^{-1/2}-t(\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}\right)^{-3/2}\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V},
$$
and evaluated at $t=0$, we obtain $\left.\frac{d}{dt}R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{orth}}(t\mathbf{V})\right|_{t=0} = \mathbf{V}$ so that the descent direction along the tangent space is preserved.

For oblique rotation, a suitable retraction involves normalizing the columns of $\mathbf{Z}$: 
$$
R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{Z} \left[\mathrm{ddiag}\!\left(\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z}\right)\right]^{-1/2},
$$ {#eq-oblq_retraction}
which is the projection used by @jennrich_2002 [Appendix A.1].

At $t=0$ we have $R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{X}$ because the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are already unit norm. To prove the second condition, we rewrite the normalization using @eq-cross_step_oblq such that
$$
R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(t\mathbf{V}) = (\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\operatorname{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})\right)^{-1/2}.
$$
Then the derivative with respect to $t$ is
$$
\frac{d}{dt}R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(t\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{V}\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\operatorname{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})\right)^{-1/2}-t(\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})\left(\mathbf{I}+t^2\operatorname{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})\right)^{-3/2}\operatorname{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}),
$$
which evaluated at $t=0$ becomes $\left.\frac{d}{dt}R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(t\mathbf{V})\right|_{t=0} = \mathbf{V}$.

Using the definitions of Riemannian gradient and retraction along with their proofs for the orthogonal and oblique cases, we are ready to develop a new rotation: the orthoblique rotation.

# The orthoblique manifold

The orthoblique manifold encompasses a mixture of oblique and orthogonal relations between factors. Geometrically, in $n=3$ it consists of solving the same problem of orthogonal and oblique rotations by minimizing a complexity function while moving vectors on a sphere, with the difference that only one vector is required to be orthogonal to the others (Figure \ref{fig:orthoblique-manifold}).
